questions.stem: Which antiretroviral targets a host-cell protein rather than a viral one?
questions.explanation: Maraviroc blocks host CCR5. A: Enfuvirtide binds viral gp41. B: Zidovudine targets reverse transcriptase. D: Raltegravir targets integrase. E: Nevirapine binds reverse transcriptase.

questions.stem: Why is amantadine ineffective against influenza B?

options.C: Influenza B has an unsegmented genome
options.E: Influenza B has NB protein instead of M2

questions.explanation: Amantadine blocks the M2 ion channel needed for uncoating; influenza B has NB instead. A: Influenza B has neuraminidase (oseltamivir works). B: It has hemagglutinin. C: Its RNA has 8 segments. D: It is enveloped.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with recurrent herpes labialis no longer responds to acyclovir. Which enzyme change most likely explains this?

options.A: Mutated or absent viral thymidine kinase

questions.explanation: Acyclovir needs viral TK for its first phosphorylation; TK mutations cause resistance (foscarnet is then used). B: Cellular TK doesn't activate acyclovir. C: UL97 activates ganciclovir in CMV. D, E: These aren't herpes targets.

questions.stem: Which anti-herpes drug requires no phosphorylation to act?
questions.explanation: Foscarnet directly inhibits viral polymerases. A, E: Need viral TK. B: Needs UL97. C: Needs cellular kinases.

questions.stem: How does oseltamivir limit influenza infection?

options.E: Blocks fusion of the envelope with the cell

questions.explanation: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir oral, zanamivir inhaled) trap new virions on the cell. A: HA attachment is not its target. C: That is amantadine. D: Not its target. E: Fusion inhibition is enfuvirtide (HIV gp41).

questions.stem: Zidovudine and nevirapine both inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase. How does zidovudine differ?

options.A: It must be phosphorylated in the cell and terminates the proviral DNA chain
options.B: It binds the enzyme directly and alters its active site
options.C: It blocks integrase from inserting proviral DNA
options.D: It binds gp41 and prevents membrane fusion
options.E: It binds CCR5 on the host cell

questions.explanation: Zidovudine is an NRTI: a nucleoside analog phosphorylated to a fake nucleotide that stops chain elongation. B: That is nevirapine (NNRTI). C: Integrase inhibitors (raltegravir). D: Enfuvirtide. E: Maraviroc.

questions.stem: How do type I interferons released by a virus-infected cell protect neighboring cells?

options.A: They neutralize free virions in the blood
options.B: They activate macrophages as their main action
options.C: They induce proteins that degrade viral mRNA and block viral protein synthesis

questions.explanation: Type I IFN (α, β) binds neighboring cells and induces an antiviral state (viral mRNA degradation, blocked viral protein synthesis) and raises MHC expression. A: Antibodies neutralize virions. B: Macrophage activation is mainly type II (IFN-γ). D: That is maraviroc. E: That is oseltamivir/zanamivir.

questions.stem: Why do influenza A and hepatitis C virus develop antiviral resistance faster than herpesviruses?

options.C: They use host DNA polymerase for replication
options.D: They become latent in sensory neurons

questions.explanation: RNA polymerases lack proofreading, giving high error rates and many resistance mutations. A: RNA viruses have small genomes (<30 kb). B: Faster, not slower, replication increases mutations. C: DNA viruses use host machinery with proofreading, so they mutate less. D: Latency is a herpesvirus feature and does not drive resistance.
